title: Codebase interviews
summary: Some interviews hand you an unfamiliar repository instead of a blank editor. You get 45 to 60 minutes to fix a bug or add a small feature while the interviewer watches how you find your way around, test your ideas and explain your choices. This guide gives you a repeatable seven-step routine and six small practice codebases to rehearse it on.

steps.title: Clarify the task
body: Repeat the task back in your own words before you open a file. Ask what 'done' looks like: a passing test, a behaviour you can demonstrate, or a written explanation.
Check the ground rules. Can you search the web or use an AI assistant? Are you expected to run the tests? Is there a part of the code you should leave alone?
checklist: Restated the task in one or two sentences
Agreed what counts as finished
Confirmed which tools are allowed

steps.title: Orient yourself
body: Read the README first, then skim the dependency list and the folder layout. Find the entry point and the tests that cover the area you will touch.
Run the existing tests before changing anything so you know the baseline. Then search for words from the task (an error message, a function name, a field) to find where the behaviour lives.
checklist: Read the README and the layout
Found the entry point and the relevant tests
Ran the suite once to get a baseline
Searched for clues from the task

steps.title: Reproduce or find a pattern
body: For a bug, write a small failing test that shows the problem. A red test proves you understand the report and later proves the fix.
For a feature, find the closest existing feature and copy its shape: where it lives, how it is named, how it is tested. Write the first test for the new behaviour before the code.
checklist: Bug: a failing test that shows the problem
Feature: a similar feature found and its pattern noted
The new test fails for the right reason

steps.title: Trace one hypothesis at a time
body: Follow the data from the test into the code. Form one guess about where it goes wrong, check it, and either confirm it or rule it out before forming the next one.
Say each hypothesis out loud. 'I think the counter is not reset after the window ends; let me check where it is set' gives the interviewer something to follow and help with.
checklist: Stated each hypothesis before checking it
Ruled hypotheses in or out with evidence
Found the root cause, not just the symptom

steps.title: Make the smallest change
body: Fix the root cause with the smallest change that does the job. Match the naming, error handling and layout of the code around it so the change reads as if it had always been there.
If you spot a refactor or an unrelated bug, write it down and mention it at the end rather than doing it now.
checklist: Changed the root cause, not a symptom
Matched the existing style
Noted refactors instead of doing them

steps.title: Verify
body: Run your new test, then the whole suite. A fix that breaks something else is not finished.
Think about edge cases: empty input, the boundary value, the second call, the error path. Add a test for the one most likely to bite.
checklist: New test passes
Full suite passes
Checked the edge cases

steps.title: Wrap up
body: Summarise in a few sentences: what caused the problem, what you changed and why, and any trade-offs you made.
Finish with what you would do with more time and anything else you noticed along the way. This is often the part interviewers remember.
checklist: Explained the cause and the fix
Named the trade-offs
Said what you would do with more time
Mentioned anything else you noticed

throughout: Narrate as you go. Silence makes it hard for the interviewer to give you credit or a nudge.
Work in small steps and commit (or run the tests) after each one so you can always get back to green.
If you are stuck for more than five minutes, say what you have ruled out and ask for a hint. Asking well is a skill being assessed.
If AI tools are allowed, use them for lookups and boilerplate, but read and test everything they produce. You own the result.

rubric.title: Orientation
levels: Started editing without reading the task or the code.
Read some code but missed the tests or the entry point.
Clarified the task, read the README and ran the baseline.
Quickly built a clear map of the code and used search to go straight to the right place.

rubric.title: Debugging
levels: Changed code at random hoping something would work.
Found the area but without a test or a clear hypothesis.
Reproduced the problem with a test and traced it to the cause.
Tested one clear hypothesis at a time and reached the root cause efficiently.

rubric.title: Code change
levels: Change does not work or breaks other tests.
Works for the main case but patches a symptom or ignores the style.
Small, correct fix in the existing style with a regression test.
Minimal root-cause fix, edge cases tested, full suite green.

rubric.title: Communication
levels: Worked in silence and gave no summary.
Explained some steps but the reasoning was hard to follow.
Narrated hypotheses and gave a clear summary at the end.
Easy to follow throughout, asked for help well and named trade-offs and next steps.
